1.pericope_label: Samuel also said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people, over Israel: now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass. And Saul gathered the people together, and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen, and ten thousand men of Judah. And Saul came to a city of Amalek, and laid wait in the valley. And Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites. And Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, that is over against Egypt. And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword. But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the Amalekites in their place and history: a fierce, untameable race of wanderers who roamed at large through the deserts between southern Judea and the Egyptian frontier, descended from Esau's grandson, who not long after the exodus attacked and cruelly harassed the almost defenceless rear-guard of Israel in the desert, were then defeated at the prayer of Moses but for that cowardly unprovoked attack solemnly doomed to destruction, and are alluded to in the prophecy of Balaam as the first of the nations who opposed the Lord's people; during the stormy ages that followed, the hand of Amalek seems to have been constantly lifted against Israel. On the command he gives the philology first, that for utterly destroy the Hebrew has the far stronger expression, to put under the ban, whatever was so put being devoted to God and incapable of redemption but to be slain, human beings and cattle killed and whatever could be burnt burnt. He then meets the moral question directly and refuses it: the cup of iniquity in this people was filled up, and its national existence, if prolonged, would simply have worked mischief to the commonwealth of nations; Israel here was simply the instrument of destruction used by the Almighty, and it is vain to attempt in this and similar transactions to find materials for the blame or the praise of Israel, since we must never forget that the nation stood in a peculiar relation to the unseen King and was not unfrequently used as the visible scourge by which the All-Wise punished hopelessly hardened sinners and deprived them of the power of working mischief. The muster-place he reports two ways, one authority identifying it with a town on the south border of Judah near the region where the Amalekites chiefly dwelt, another denying it was a town at all, since the name signifies lambs and a word for house is probably to be understood, so that it was some open spot where at the proper season the lambs were collected from the pastures in the wilderness. Judah's contingent he notes is again out of proportion to the numbers furnished by the rest of the tribes. The city he would render not a city of Amalek but the city, no doubt their principal place of arms, and the valley a torrent bed then dry; and he reports a strange tradition that Saul's mind misgave him when he came to this torrent bed, calling to mind the command to slay a heifer at a torrent in expiation of a murder, and determining to spare rather than to slay. The Kenites he describes as a nomad race like the Amalekites but ever friendly to the Israelites, the kindly feeling springing up soon after the departure from Egypt and owing in the first instance to the father-in-law of Moses belonging to this people. Of the two boundaries he can identify only one, since the first cannot now be fixed, while the second signifies wall and probably refers to the wall which crossed the north-east frontier of Egypt. The sparing he divides by motive: Saul seems to have carried out the curse to the letter in the case of the human beings and the less valuable beasts, but covetousness seems to have suggested the preservation of the choicest cattle, and pride probably induced him to save Agag alive that he might show the people his royal captive. Delitzsch frames the chapter by the earlier failure: as Saul had transgressed the commandment of God given through Samuel by the sacrifice at Gilgal at the very commencement of his reign, and had thereby drawn upon himself the threat that his monarchy should not be continued in perpetuity, so his disobedience in this war was followed by his rejection on the part of God. He rehearses the ground of the sentence, that the Amalekites were the first heathen nation to attack Israel after the deliverance from Egypt, and did it in the most treacherous manner, for which they had been threatened with extermination, Moses enjoining this upon Joshua and also committing it to writing for all future generations; and since they afterwards manifested the same hostility on every favourable occasion, the Lord now instructed Samuel to issue the command. Of the divine resolve he says that when God looks upon a sin, directing his glance towards it, he must punish it according to his own holiness, and that the Hebrew verb points at the very outset to the punishment about to be proclaimed. The numbers he defends rather than questions: they are not too large, for a powerful Bedouin nation such as the Amalekites were could not possibly be attacked successfully with a small army but only by raising the whole of the military force of Israel, and the text implies that the two hundred thousand were from the other tribes. On the ambush he is careful: the verb does not come from the root meaning to fight or quarrel but was understood even by the early translators as a contracted form of the causative of the root meaning to lie in wait, and modern commentators have generally understood it in the same way, though one scholar questions the reading and another proposes an emendation. Of the extermination he says that all means all that fell into the hands of the Israelites, for it follows from the very nature of the case that many escaped, and consequently there is nothing striking in Amalekites being mentioned again at a later period, the last remnant being destroyed upon the mountains of Seir in the reign of Hezekiah.

Gill supplies the framework from Jewish tradition, that blotting out the name and memory of Amalek was reckoned one of the three things the Israelites were obliged to do when they came into the land of Canaan, the others being to appoint a king over them and to build the house of the sanctuary, and that this work was reserved for Saul, their first king. The title of the Lord of hosts he expounds as of the celestial host of angels, of the army of Israel, and indeed of all the armies of the earth, premised in order to engage Saul's attention. The gathering he explains as making the people hear, by the sound of a trumpet or by sending heralds into all parts of the land to proclaim the order of the Lord and summon them. On the city he reports both views, that Saul came with his army perhaps to the nearest city of Amalek to the land of Israel, though some think Amalek was the name of the city and the metropolis of the nation, named from the people; and of the valley he gives three renderings, that Saul laid wait there, or contended and fought there, or, with the Targum, ordered his army and pitched his camp there. The Kenites he identifies as of the posterity or kindred of the father-in-law of Moses, and confesses himself at a loss why the Jewish historian calls them by another name altogether and places them in the midst of Midian. The sparing of Agag he attributes to Saul's own motion, the people agreeing to it, and offers three possible reasons, respect to him as a king, the comeliness of his person with the height of his stature and the largeness of his body, and the design of carrying him in triumph in a public show.

Clarke gives the chapter's argument at the head and then praises the king without qualification, that he was one of the best, if not the best, of all the Jewish kings since the time of David, and that he began well, continued well and ended well. The Amalekites he places as a people of Arabia Petraea who had occupied a tract on the frontiers of Egypt and Palestine, and who acted with great cruelty towards the Israelites coming out of Egypt, falling on them when they were faint and weary and smiting the hindmost, those too weak to keep up with the rest; God then purposed that Amalek as a nation should be blotted out from under heaven, which purpose was now fulfilled by Saul upwards of four hundred years afterwards. On the severity of the command he concedes the difficulty and rests the whole weight on authority: nothing could justify such an exterminating decree but the absolute authority of God, and this was given; all the reasons of it we do not know, but this we know well, that the Judge of all the earth does right; and he notes that the war was not for plunder, since God commanded that all the property as well as all the people should be destroyed. The numbers he surveys across the witnesses, the Greek of one great polyglot giving four hundred thousand companies of Israel and thirty thousand of Judah, one codex ten thousand of each, another edition two hundred thousand and ten thousand, and the Jewish historian four hundred thousand and thirty thousand, while all the other versions agree with the Hebrew text and the manuscripts show no variation. The summing of the silver he dates by inference, that since Josiah began to seek the Lord as soon as he began to reign, the accustomed offerings had been accumulating ten years with no account taken of them. The city he would translate not a city of Amalek but the city Amalek, their capital being called by the name of their tribe. The Kenites he calls an ancient people, noting that the father-in-law of Moses was one and that his son, if the same person be not meant, was guide to the Hebrews through the wilderness, and that they had a portion of the promised land near a city of the south. Of the two boundaries he reports the Jewish historian placing them from a city in Egypt to the Red Sea, but observes that the first lay eastward from the Red Sea while the Amalekites lay between that and the way to Egypt. Wesley reads the opening as a summons to retrieve a lost position, that Saul had committed error already and should now regain God's favour by exact obedience. The ground of the war he states as the revenging of old injuries upon children who continue in their parents' practices, and he aggravates the original crime: Israel was newly come out of cruel and long bondage, weak and weary and faint and hungry, so that instead of the pity which even nature prompted it was barbarous to add affliction to the afflicted, and it was besides horrid impiety to fight against God himself and to lift up their hand against the Lord's throne while they struck at a people God had brought forth in so stupendous a way. The hardest part of the command he does not evade but argues: the slaying was not unjust, because God is the supreme Lord of life and can require his own when he pleases; infants likewise are born in sin and therefore liable to God's wrath; their death was rather a mercy than a curse, as being the occasion of preventing their sin and punishment; and the beasts, being all made for man's benefit, may not strangely suffer with him for the instruction of mankind. The repetition of the charge he takes as designed to prevent mistake and to oblige Saul to exact performance. The Kenites he derives from or relates to the father-in-law of Moses, has them anciently dwelling in rocks near the Amalekites and afterwards in Judah, whence it is probable they removed back to their old habitation, dwelling in tents and able easily to do so, because of the wars with which Judah was annoyed; and he notes that it was some of their progenitors who showed the kindness, for whose sakes all of them should fare the better, since they were not guilty of the sin for which Amalek was now to be destroyed. Of the smiting he says Saul smote all that he met with, but a great number fled away upon the noise of his coming and secured themselves in other places till the storm was over; and of the sparing he draws the rule, that they obeyed God only so far as they could without inconvenience to themselves.

Henry reads the commission as a deliberate trial, and says that the making of this so expressly the trial of Saul's obedience did very much aggravate his disobedience. He draws out the argument from gratitude that Samuel puts first: the Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king, God gave thee thy power and therefore expects thou shouldst use it for him, he put honour upon thee and now thou must study to do him honour, he made thee king over Israel and now thou must plead Israel's cause and avenge their quarrels, thou art advanced to command Israel but art a subject to the God of Israel; and he generalises it, that men's preferment, instead of releasing them from their obedience to God, obliges them so much the more to it, and that God's favours to us lay strong obligations upon us to be obedient. Of the ancient quarrel he draws five notes: that injuries done to God's Israel will certainly be reckoned for sooner or later, especially the opposition given them when they were coming out of Egypt; that God often bears long with those that are marked for ruin, the sentence passed not being speedily executed; that though he bear long he will not bear always, since the year of recompence for the controversy of Israel will come at last, and though divine justice strikes slowly it strikes surely; that the longer judgment is delayed the more severe it often is when it comes; and that God chooses out instruments to do his work that are fittest for it, this being bloody work and therefore Saul, who was a rough and severe man, must do it. On the muster he contrasts the numbers with an earlier war, that when Saul engaged the Philistines and the success was hazardous he had but six hundred attending him, whereas now, when he was to attack the Amalekites by express order from heaven and was sure of victory, he had thousands at his call; but he finds Judah's quota scandalously short, a twentieth part of the whole, and says that whatever it was at other times it was not now for the honour of Judah that their forces were numbered by themselves, the day of Judah's honour drawing near but not yet come. The place of muster he reads through the old versions, that the name signifies lambs, so that the Latin has Saul number them like lambs and the Chaldee by the paschal lambs, allowing ten men to a lamb, which he notes was a way of numbering used by the Jews in the later times of their nation. The warning to the Kenites he judges prudent and pious, and probably given according to Samuel's direction. He makes much of the acknowledgement of their ancestors' kindness: a good man leaves the divine blessing for an inheritance to his children's children, and those who come after us may be reaping the benefit of our good works when we are in our graves; God is not unrighteous to forget the kindnesses shown to his people, which shall be remembered another day and recompensed in the resurrection of the just; and God's remembering the kindness of the Kenites' ancestors at the very time when he was punishing the injuries done by the ancestors of the Amalekites helped to clear the righteousness of God in the dispensation, since if he entail favours, why may he not entail frowns? The removal he turns to use, that when destroying judgments are abroad God will take care to separate between the precious and the vile and to hide the meek of the earth in the day of his anger, so that it is dangerous to be found in the company of God's enemies and it is our duty and interest to come out from among them lest we share in their sins and plagues; and he quotes the Jewish saying, woe to the wicked man and woe to his neighbour. The victory itself he calls rather an execution of condemned malefactors than a war with contending enemies, the issue not being dubious when the cause was just and the call so clear; and he marvels at the ground of the reckoning, that though the Amalekites were idolaters and guilty of many other sins for which they deserved to fall under God's wrath, yet when God would reckon with them he fastened upon the sin of their ancestors in abusing his Israel as the ground of his quarrel, so that he exclaims how unsearchable are God's judgments and yet how incontestable his righteousness. The half-done work he analyses by motive, that Saul spared Agag because he was a king like himself and perhaps in hope of a great ransom, and spared the best of the cattle while destroying the refuse that was good for little; and he puts the sting in it, that what was now destroyed was in effect sacrificed to the justice of God as the God to whom vengeance belongs, so that for Saul to think the torn and the sick, the lame and the lean, good enough for that, while he reserved the firstlings and the fat for his own fields and his own table, was really to honour himself more than God. Many of the people, he supposes, made their escape and took their effects with them into other countries, and therefore we read of Amalekites after this, but that could not be helped; it was Saul's fault that he did not destroy such as came to his hands and were in his power.

debates: How so sweeping a sentence of extermination is to be justified, where Clarke concedes the difficulty and rests the whole weight on authority, that nothing could justify such a decree but the absolute authority of God, which was given, so that though all the reasons are unknown to us we know well that the Judge of all the earth does right; Ellicott refuses the question itself as improper, since it is vain in such transactions to look for materials for the blame or the praise of Israel, which stood in a peculiar relation to the unseen King and was used as the visible scourge by which the All-Wise punished hopelessly hardened sinners; Wesley argues it out point by point instead, that God is the supreme Lord of life and may require his own, that infants are born in sin and so liable to wrath, that their death was rather a mercy than a curse as preventing their sin and its punishment, and that the beasts, made for man's benefit, may suffer with him; and Delitzsch grounds it in the divine nature, that when God looks upon a sin he must punish it according to his own holiness.

What the numbers of the muster were and whether they are credible, where Clarke lays out the variant witnesses, the Greek of one polyglot giving four hundred thousand companies of Israel and thirty thousand of Judah, one codex ten thousand of each, another edition two hundred thousand and ten thousand, and the Jewish historian four hundred thousand and thirty thousand, while the rest agree with the Hebrew; Henry and Ellicott both find Judah's ten thousand scandalously out of proportion to the other tribes, Henry calling it a twentieth part of the whole and saying that Judah's day of honour drew near but was not yet come; and Delitzsch defends the Hebrew total as not too large at all, since a powerful Bedouin nation could not be attacked successfully with a small army but only by raising the whole military force of Israel.

Why Saul spared what he spared, where Henry assigns the sparing of Agag to his being a king like Saul himself and perhaps to the hope of a great ransom, and the sparing of the cattle to covetousness, so that reserving the fat for his own table while offering the lame and the lean to God's justice was to honour himself more than God; Ellicott agrees about the covetousness but makes the sparing of Agag a matter of pride, that the king might show the people his royal captive; Gill offers the same with the comeliness of Agag's person and the design of a public triumph added; and Wesley reduces the whole to a rule, that they obeyed God only so far as they could without inconvenience to themselves.
outliers: Ellicott reports a strange tradition that Saul's mind misgave him at the dry torrent bed, where he called to mind the command to slay a heifer at a torrent in expiation of a murder, and determined to spare rather than to slay.

Henry and Delitzsch agree against the letter of the text that many Amalekites escaped, Henry supposing they carried their effects into other countries, which could not be helped, and Delitzsch that it follows from the nature of the case, so that there is nothing striking in Amalekites appearing again long afterwards.
