10.pericope_label: Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel, saying, It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king: for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. And it grieved Samuel; and he cried unto the Lord all night. And when Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning, it was told Samuel, saying, Saul came to Carmel, and, behold, he set him up a place, and is gone about, and passed on, and gone down to Gilgal. And Samuel came to Saul: and Saul said unto him, Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord. And Samuel said, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear? And Saul said, They have brought them from the Amalekites: for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. Then Samuel said unto Saul, Stay, and I will tell thee what the Lord hath said to me this night. And he said unto him, Say on. And Samuel said, When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel? And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed. Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? And Saul said unto Samuel, Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal. And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.

schools.summary: Ellicott thinks the word came to Samuel very likely in a dream, and on the divine repentance quotes an earlier authority to the effect that God does not feel the pain of remorse, nor is ever deceived so as to desire to correct anything in which he has erred, but that as a man desires to make a change when he repents, so when God is said in Scripture to repent we may expect a change from him, he having changed Saul's kingdom when he is said to have repented of making him king. Of Samuel's grief he quotes a reformer at length, that many grave thoughts seem to have presented themselves at once and disturbed his mind when he reflected on the dishonour which would be inflicted upon the name of God, and the occasion which the rejection and deposition of Saul would furnish to wicked men for blaspheming the invisible King of Israel, since Saul had been chosen by God himself from all the people and called by him to the throne, so that if he were deposed it seemed likely the worship of God would be overturned and the greatest disturbance ensue. The monument he locates at a place in Judah to the south-east of Hebron and reads its name literally as a hand, comparing a pillar elsewhere styled a hand rather than a place, and suggesting that very likely these victory cairns or columns erected by the Hebrews had a hand engraved upon them. Of Saul's greeting he says the king must have been fully conscious that he had failed to carry out the will and command of the eternal King of Israel, having in a war undertaken for the definite and solemn purpose of exterminating a wicked and bloodthirsty people disregarded the express instructions of the prophet for his own covetous purposes; conscious of all this he still dared to come forward and congratulate the prophet upon the fulfilment of the Lord's command, so that his words of self-gratulation were evidently feigned. The conviction by the animals he gives in another's words, that Saul is convicted of falsehood by the voices of the creatures he has spared contrary to God's command, and that Samuel's mode of citing them against him has an air of holy humour and cutting irony. The excuse he reconstructs as speech: at once the king understood the drift of his old friend's words, and still more the stern sorrowful look of reproach which accompanied them, and answered that the bleating did indeed come from the captured flocks of Amalek but that the reservation was insisted upon by the people, whose object was to do special honour to God in a great sacrifice; and Ellicott finds something strangely cowardly in this trying to transfer the blame from himself to the people, unlike Saul's old character, but adds that covetousness and vanity invariably lead to moral cowardice. The command to stay he reads dramatically, the king probably turning away in desire to close an interview full of bitterness when he was arrested by the solemn words and probably by the commanding gesture of his old friend and counsellor, who now addressed him with the majesty and power of an accredited servant of the Most High. On the reminder of his former smallness he reports and rejects a rendering which would make the sense that though Saul seemed to himself too little and weak to curb the people he was nevertheless the head and should have done his duty, on the ground that this would imply Samuel had accepted the excuse that it was the people's will to reserve the choicest spoil; the prophet's words were simply to remind Saul that the Lord whose expressed will he had disregarded had raised him from a comparatively humble station, there having been a time when he judged himself unequal to the work, whereas now, flushed with success, he was trusting in his unaided strength. The flying upon the spoil he says evidently includes the idea of greedy eagerness, as though Samuel detected a spirit of grasping covetousness at the bottom of the act; and the repetition of the excuse shows the state of Saul's mind, since he evidently disbelieved in the power of the Eternal as a heart-reader and cared only to justify himself before Samuel, asserting his own integrity of purpose and his zeal for the public sacrifice while knowing all the while that low earthly reasons had been the springs of his conduct. On the great saying he hears the Spirit of the Lord descending upon Samuel in one of those rapt expressions which these prophets were now and again commissioned to give out, and traces it forward through the Psalms and Isaiah and Jeremiah and Micah and Hosea, and into our Lord's own words; he quotes one father for seeing in it a plain intimation that the day would come when the burnt offerings enjoined on Israel would give place to a simple worship of the heart, and another for the weighty comment that in sacrifices a man offers only strange flesh whereas in obedience he offers his own will. The last verse he expounds as the ground of the rejection: witchcraft, more literally soothsaying or divination, was the greatest of all the dangers to which Israel was exposed and was in fact a tampering with the idol-worship of the surrounding nations, whose various systems were characterised by impurity and an utter lack of the loftier principles of morality; so that rebellion, or conscious disobedience to the express commands of the Eternal in the case of God's chosen king, was nothing else than the deadly sin of idol-worship, for it set aside the true Master of Israel and virtually acknowledged another, and stubbornness or intractableness is in the eyes of the pure God the same thing as worshipping idols and household gods; the Hebrew word rendered iniquity, he adds, literally signifies nothingness. Delitzsch states the word of the Lord plainly and then guards it, that it does not express any changeableness in the divine nature but simply the sorrow of the divine love at the rebellion of sinners, as is evident enough from a later verse of the chapter; to turn round from following God in order to go his own ways was Saul's real sin, since he would no longer be the follower and servant of the Lord but would be absolute ruler in Israel, pride arising from the consciousness of his own strength leading him astray to break the command of God.

Gill guards the divine repentance as carefully as the others: it is not to be understood of any change of mind, counsel, purpose or decree in God, which is not consistent with his unchangeable nature, but of a change of dispensation and outward dealings, and is spoken after the manner of men, who when they repent of anything change the course of their conduct and behaviour; so the Lord does without any change of his mind and will, which alters not, and though he changes the outward dispensations of his providence he never changes in the matters and methods of his grace, so that though he repented that he made Saul king he never repents of the gifts of his grace. The prophet's early rising he explains by his sleeplessness, that he had had no rest since the revelation of the will of God was made to him and therefore rose early, being in haste to speak with Saul. The excuse he treats as the oldest of evasions, Saul laying the blame upon the people as Adam did upon his wife, as if he had no concern at all in it when it is clear that he was the principal one, nor is it probable the people should have done this of themselves without his consent and authority, which was so directly contrary to the express order of God; and then, to excuse as well as he could the people on whom he laid the blame, he observed that it was not done for their own private profit but for the service and worship of God. The command to stay he reads as a courtesy, that Samuel, Saul being a king, treats him as such and asks audience of him, or leave to deliver what he had to say. The reminder of his smallness he glosses as his having been humble and lowly with a mean opinion of himself, his family and his tribe, judging himself unworthy of the kingdom, with the suggestion that now he was proud and haughty and would have his own will and way. Saul's protest he treats as an interruption, Saul breaking in upon Samuel before he had declared all that the Lord had said, unable to forbear when he heard himself charged with not obeying, and affirming with the utmost assurance that he had obeyed, though poor proof does he give of it; and still he continues to lay the blame on the people, when he as king ought to have restrained them. The last verse he expounds by the law, that rebellion against God or disobeying his commands, even in things otherwise lawful were they not forbidden, is as heinous a sin as to be guilty of witchcraft or any kind of divination forbidden by the law of God, and deserves as sore a punishment.

Clarke explains the divine repentance as a change of purpose according to conditions already laid down or mentally determined: God placed Saul on the throne and intended, had he been obedient, to have established his kingdom, but he has been disobedient, and so God changes his purpose and the kingdom shall not be established in his family. The monument he reads literally as a hand, reporting that some say it was a monument and others a triumphal arch, but thinking it probably no more than a hand pointing out the place where Saul had gained the victory, and comparing the pillar elsewhere called a hand. On the excuse he is willing to concede the fact while fixing the guilt: it is very likely that the people did spare the best of the prey, and it is as likely that Saul might have restrained them if he would, and he notes the reason for the original interdict, that God had forbidden spoil and plunder so that they might not love war and the war might be undertaken merely from a sense of duty without any hope of enriching themselves by it. The reminder of Saul's former smallness he turns into a question about prosperity, asking who can bear it, and whether it is not of the Lord's great goodness that the majority of the inhabitants of the earth are in comparative poverty. The plea of sacrifice he states as Saul's attempt to excuse the people, that they did not take the spoil in order to enrich themselves but to sacrifice to the Lord, and asks whether that motive did not justify their conduct; and he calls Samuel's reply a very proper answer to the excuse and a refutation of it, asking whether obedience to the will of God is not the end of all religion, of its rites and ceremonies and sacrifices. The last verse he will not read as the received version gives it, which he says is no translation of those difficult words, and he observes that all the versions are different; his own proposal is that the three nouns occurring first in the text refer each to the three last in order, transgression to iniquity, which is the principle whence transgression springs, divination to the consecrated images used in incantations, and rebellion to stubbornness, whence rebellion springs, so that the meaning is that as transgression comes from iniquity, divination from the images and rebellion from stubbornness, so, because Saul had rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord had also rejected him from being king. Wesley reasons about the repentance from the term, that it implies grief of heart and change of counsels and therefore cannot be in God, but is ascribed to him when he alters his method of dealing and treats a person as if he did indeed repent of the kindness he had shown him; the night of prayer he takes as imploring pardoning mercy for Saul and for the people; and from the phrase about turning back he draws the inference that Saul did once follow God, since otherwise it would have been impossible that he should turn back from following him. The monument he calls a trophy of the victory. Saul's second plea he reads as a conscience half awake, beginning to stir though but a little, since he still lays the blame on the people. On the great saying he distinguishes the two kinds of command: obedience to God is a moral duty, constantly and indispensably necessary, whereas sacrifice is but a ceremonial institution, sometimes unnecessary, as it was in the wilderness, and sometimes sinful, when offered by a polluted hand or in an irregular manner, so that gross disobedience to God's express command is not to be compensated with sacrifice. The terms of the last verse he glosses one by one, rebellion as disobedience to God's command, stubbornness as contumacy in sin, justifying it and pleading for it, and iniquity as the iniquity of idolatry; and of the rejection he makes a careful distinction, that God had pronounced the sentence of rejection but had not actually deposed Saul before, as plainly appears from the fact that not only the people but even David afterwards owned him as king.

Henry takes the passage as remarkable instances both of the strictness of the justice of God and of the treachery and deceitfulness of the heart of man. The divine repentance he qualifies at once: repentance in God is not, as it is in us, a change of his mind, but a change of his method or dispensation, so that he does not alter his will but wills an alteration, the change being in Saul, who has turned back from following God, which construction God himself puts upon the partiality of his obedience and the prevalency of his covetousness; and Henry marks the limit, that God repented he had given Saul the kingdom and the honour and power belonging to it, but never repented that he had given any man wisdom and grace and his fear and love, these gifts and callings being without repentance. Samuel's lamenting he describes with evident feeling: it grieved him that Saul had forfeited God's favour and that God had resolved to cast him off, and he cried unto the Lord all night, spending a whole night in interceding that the decree might not go forth, so that when others were in their beds sleeping he was upon his knees praying and wrestling with God; he did not deprecate his own exclusion from the government, nor was he secretly pleased, as many a one would have been, that Saul who succeeded him was so soon laid aside, but on the contrary prayed earnestly for his establishment, so far was he from desiring that woeful day; and Henry draws the rule, that the rejection of sinners is the grief of good people, since God delights not in their death, nor should we. Of the meeting at Gilgal he notes that this was the place where Saul was made king and where he would now have been confirmed had he approved himself well in the trial of his obedience, and that Samuel was informed Saul had set up a triumphal arch or monument of his victory, seeking his own honour more than the honour of God, when he had more need to have been repenting of his sin and making his peace with God than boasting of his victory. Saul's boast he reads as a pre-emption: it is very likely that if his conscience had flown in his face he would not have been so forward to proclaim his obedience, for by this he hoped to prevent Samuel's reproving him; thus sinners think, by justifying themselves, to escape being judged of the Lord, whereas the only way to do that is by judging ourselves, and those that boast most of their religion may be suspected of partiality and hypocrisy in it. The conviction Henry makes almost physical: Saul would have it thought that God Almighty was wonderfully beholden to him, but Samuel shows that God was so far from being a debtor to him that he had just cause of action against him, and produces for evidence the bleating of the sheep and the lowing of the oxen, which perhaps Saul appointed to bring up the rear of his triumph but which Samuel calls as witnesses against him; he needed not go far to disprove his professions, for the noise the cattle made, like the rust of silver, would be a witness against him, and Henry turns this on the reader, that it is no new thing for the plausible professions of hypocrites to be disproved by the most plain and undeniable evidence, since many boast of their obedience while their indulgence of the flesh, their love of the world, their passion and uncharitableness and their neglect of holy duties witness against them. The excuse he takes apart in two pieces, that it was not his fault because the people spared them, as if they durst have done it without his express orders when they knew it was against Samuel's express orders, from which Henry draws that those who are willing to justify themselves are commonly very forward to condemn others, and that sin is a brat that nobody cares to have laid at his doors; and that it was with a good intention, which he calls a false plea since both Saul and the people designed their own profit, and frivolous even if it had been true, since God hates robbery for burnt-offering, having appointed these cattle to be sacrificed in the field, so that he will give no thanks to those who bring them to his altar, for he will be served in his own way, and a good intention will not justify a bad action. Of the judgment Henry notes that Samuel premised his authority, since what he was about to say was what the Lord had said to him, and that those who complain their ministers are too harsh should remember that while they keep to the word of God they are but messengers and must say as they are bidden. The honour God had done Saul he presses, that he was made king when he was little in his own sight, God regarding the lowness of his state and rewarding the lowliness of his spirit, so that those advanced to honour and wealth ought often to remember their mean beginnings. The plainness of the orders he urges too, that the service was so easy and the success so certain that it was rather to be called a journey than a war, and that had Saul denied himself and set aside the consideration of his own profit he would have been no loser at last, God no doubt making it up to him; and he exclaims at the love of money, asking what evil it is not the root of, and finding in disobedience the thing which above anything else makes sin evil in the sight of the Lord. Saul's repeated vindication he treats as the hardening of conviction into resolve, Saul denying the charge because he had done all he thought he needed to do, so much wiser was he in his own eyes than God himself, and putting among the instances of his obedience that he had brought Agag alive, which he thought as good as killing him, so that carnal deceitful hearts think to excuse themselves from God's commandments with their own equivalents; Henry grants that Saul knew his Lord's will and was under no mistake about the command, but thought the destruction wilful waste, the cattle of another nation having been taken for a prey in Moses's time, and better that it should be prey to the Israelites than to the fowls of the air, so that he connived at the people's carrying it away; and he concludes how hard a thing it is to convince the children of disobedience of their sin and to strip them of their fig-leaves. On the great answer Henry appeals to conscience and then expounds it at length: nothing is so pleasing to God as obedience, not sacrifice and offering nor the fat of rams, and a careful conformity to moral precepts recommends us to God more than all ceremonial observances, since obedience is enjoined by the eternal law of nature but sacrifice only by a positive law, obedience was the law of innocency while sacrifice supposes sin come into the world and is but a feeble attempt to take away what obedience would have prevented, and God is more glorified and self more denied by obedience than by sacrifice, it being much easier to bring a bullock or lamb to be burnt upon the altar than to bring every high thought into obedience to God and the will subject to his will, so that obedience is the glory of angels and will be ours. And nothing is so provoking to God as disobedience, setting up our wills in competition with his, which is here called rebellion and stubbornness and is said to be as bad as witchcraft and idolatry, since it is as bad to set up other gods as to live in disobedience to the true God, and those governed by their own corrupt inclinations in opposition to the command of God do in effect consult the household images or the diviners; it was disobedience that made us all sinners, and this is the malignity of sin, that it is the transgression of the law and consequently enmity to God. Saul was a king, Henry adds, but if he disobey the command of God his royal dignity will not excuse him from the guilt of rebellion and stubbornness, and he marks precisely what the text speaks of, not the rebellion of the people against their prince but of a prince against God; those are unfit and unworthy to rule over men who are not willing that God should rule over them.

debates: How the statement that God repents is to be understood, where Henry calls it not a change of his mind but of his method, so that he does not alter his will but wills an alteration; Gill says the same and adds the limit, that though God repented of making Saul king he never repents of the gifts of his grace; Clarke makes it conditional, a change of purpose according to conditions already laid down, since God had intended to establish the kingdom had Saul been obedient; Wesley argues from the term, that repentance implies grief of heart and change of counsels and therefore cannot be in God but is ascribed to him when he alters his method; Delitzsch grounds it in the text, that the words express no changeableness in the divine nature but the sorrow of divine love at the rebellion of sinners; and Ellicott quotes an earlier authority to the effect that God feels no remorse and is never deceived so as to wish to correct an error of his own, but that where Scripture says he repents we may expect a change from him.

What the last verse of the tile says and how it should be rendered, where Ellicott, Henry, Gill and Wesley all keep the plain equation and make rebellion as the sin of divination and stubbornness as idolatry, Ellicott adding that conscious disobedience in God's chosen king set aside the true Master of Israel and virtually acknowledged another, and Henry that those governed by their own corrupt inclinations in effect consult the household images; against them all Clarke denies that the received version is a translation of the words at all, observes that all the versions differ, and proposes that the three nouns of the first half answer each to the three of the second, transgression to iniquity, divination to the consecrated images, and rebellion to stubbornness, so that the sense is that as each springs from the other, so, because Saul rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord rejected him from being king.

On what ground obedience is preferred to sacrifice, where Henry rests it on the order of the two laws, obedience being enjoined by the eternal law of nature and sacrifice only by a positive law, obedience the law of innocency while sacrifice supposes sin already in the world and is a feeble attempt to take away what obedience would have prevented; Wesley makes the same distinction as moral against ceremonial, sacrifice being sometimes unnecessary and sometimes sinful when offered by a polluted hand; Clarke puts it as a question, whether obedience to the will of God is not the end of all religion with its rites and ceremonies and sacrifices; and Ellicott hears the Spirit descending on Samuel in a rapt utterance, tracing the saying forward through the later prophets and into our Lord's own words.
outliers: Ellicott reconstructs the confrontation as drama, with Saul turning away to close an interview full of bitterness and being arrested by the solemn words and probably the commanding gesture of his old friend, and quotes a commentator for the tone of the question about the bleating, that it has an air of holy humour and cutting irony.

Wesley distinguishes the sentence of rejection from an actual deposing, since neither the people nor even David ceased afterwards to own Saul as king, and notes that the prophet does not say Saul is rejected from salvation, asking who else has authority to say so.
themes: Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel, saying,
It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king: for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. And it grieved Samuel; and he cried unto the Lord all night.
And when Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning, it was told Samuel, saying, Saul came to Carmel, and, behold, he set him up a place, and is gone about, and passed on, and gone down to Gilgal.
And Samuel came to Saul: and Saul said unto him, Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord.
And Samuel said, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear?
And Saul said, They have brought them from the Amalekites: for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed.
Then Samuel said unto Saul, Stay, and I will tell thee what the Lord hath said to me this night. And he said unto him, Say on.
And Samuel said, When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel?
And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed.
Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord?
And Saul said unto Samuel, Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites.
But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.
And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.

24.pericope_label: And Saul said unto Samuel, I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. Now therefore, I pray thee, pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord. And Samuel said unto Saul, I will not return with thee: for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. And as Samuel turned about to go away, he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent. And Samuel said unto him, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent. Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord thy God. So Samuel turned again after Saul; and Saul worshipped the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the confession as genuine alarm imperfectly repented. The grave condemnation of the prophet appalled the king, and the grounds of the divine rejection evidently sank deep into Saul's heart, since such a thought as that in the eyes of the Invisible and Eternal he ranked with the idolaters and heathen sinners around was terrible even for one sunk so low; yet with stammering lips, while deprecating the sentence, he still seeks to justify himself, and all that he could allege in excuse only more plainly marked out his unfitness for his high post, since he could after all only plead that he loved the praise of men more than the approval of his God, preferring, as so many of earth's great ones have since done, the sweets of transient popular applause to the solitary consciousness of being a faithful servant of the Highest. The request for pardon he reads as sorrow for consequences, that Saul's grief was rather for the immediate earthly consequence he feared might follow, since he foresaw his power in Israel would sensibly decrease, and so entreats the great prophet not to desert him; and Samuel, seeing too clearly what the true springs of this repentance were, refuses at first, it being only, as Ellicott quotes an expositor for urging forcibly, a fear on the king's part of losing the kingdom and of incurring public disgrace. The seizing of the garment he describes as a passionate action indicating a restless, unquiet mind, Saul not content with entreating words laying hold of the old man as he turns away, perhaps even with some violence, in order to detain him; and he corrects the English rendering, since what Saul laid hold of and tore was not the mantle of the Authorised Version but the hem or outer border of the ordinary tunic which the upper classes in Israel were then in the habit of wearing. He supports the correction from a careful note by another writer showing that the mantle which would be the accurate rendering of the Hebrew word for the distinctive dress of the Hebrew prophets was certainly not used in the days of Samuel, the great founder of the prophetic order, special dresses having come into use only gradually, so that Elijah is the first person described as being thus clad, long after the school of the prophets had grown into a national institution. The omen he reads as taken from the accident: the prophet at once looks upon the garment torn by the king's passionate vehemence as an omen for the future and uses the rent vesture as a symbol to show Saul that thus had the Lord that day rent the kingdom from him; and the successor he notes is referred to quite indefinitely as a neighbour, since it had not yet been revealed to the seer who was to replace the rebellious king. The title in the declaration of irreversibility he would render better as the Changeless One of Israel, noting that the Hebrew word is first found in this passage and that in later Hebrew it is rendered glory from the Aramaean usage, while some less accurately translate it here the Victory or the Triumph of Israel; and he sets the two statements of the chapter side by side, that the Eternal is said earlier to repent of having set up Saul while here the Changeless One of Israel will not repent, resolving them by saying that with God there is no change, since now he approves of men and their works and promises them rich blessings and now he condemns and punishes the ways of the same men, whence he is said to repent, but the change springs alone from a change in the men themselves and not in God, the Lord being said to repent in human language because there was what appeared to be a change in the eternal counsels. The second request he judges strange penitence after all, Saul being no doubt terribly in earnest and in great fear, but his earnestness based upon a desire to maintain his power and royal state, and his fear springing from a well-grounded apprehension that if he lost the countenance of the revered seer he would probably forfeit his crown; and Ellicott quotes a father for the test of it, that if Saul had been really penitent he would have prayed to have been humble rather than to be honoured. Samuel's consenting at last he explains politically, that there is little doubt the principal motive which induced him not to withdraw from the public thanksgiving was a desire to prevent any disaffection towards the monarchy, since his known disapproval of Saul's conduct and his declining the king's earnest prayer to stay would probably have been the signal to the discontented spirits in Israel to revolt under the pretext that such a revolt would be pleasing to the great seer, which in those critical times would have been disastrous to the growing prosperity of the chosen people; and he adds the suggestion that many blessings came upon the unhappy king and his nation in answer to Samuel's intercession on this occasion, the result being that Saul remained in undiminished power apparently while the will of God was slowly but surely accomplished, the doom pronounced upon the reigning family being irrevocable. Delitzsch attends to the Hebrew of the tearing: the passive form is correct and is not to be altered, as one critic proposes on the authority of the Greek, into a reading which would make Saul tear off the lappet, and this is evident from the explanation Samuel gave of the occurrence; for as Saul was about to hold back the prophet by force in order to obtain from him a revocation of the divine sentence, the tearing of the mantle took place accidentally and evidently without any such intention. Of Samuel's yielding he says that after the declaration as to the irrevocable character of God's determination he gave way to the renewed entreaty that he would honour Saul before the elders and the people, and remained while Saul worshipped, not merely, as another writer has it, for the purpose of preserving the outward order until a new king should take his place, but also to carry out the ban upon Agag whom Saul had spared.

Gill judges the confession unsound from the first: it does not appear to be ingenuous, cordial and sincere, and was made chiefly for the sake of getting the sentence of rejection reversed. The request for pardon he reads charitably as to its theology, since it can hardly be thought Saul was so ignorant as to imagine Samuel could pardon sin committed against God, which none but God can do, but rather that he would forgive it so far as he himself had been offended, or that, being a prophet of the Lord with great interest in him, he would use that interest on Saul's behalf and pray that the sin might be forgiven. Samuel's refusal he grounds in dissatisfaction, that he was not satisfied with a repentance and confession which still extenuated the sin and laid the blame on the people, and that he spoke by way of resentment and as expressing his indignation, though he afterwards did return on a change of mind, which a good man may be allowed to make without any imputation of falsehood or a lie. Of the turning away he supposes Samuel went a different road from Gilgal, perhaps towards his own city, with the intention of having nothing more to say to Saul or to do with him, so displeased was he. The omen he reads as prophecy impressed from above, that Samuel, seeing his mantle rent by Saul, took occasion from it to predict, and no doubt it was impressed on his mind by the Spirit of God, that the kingdom should be in like manner rent from him on account of his own evil conduct, and that from this day forward he might expect it, the sentence having gone forth and not to be reversed. The declaration of irreversibility he applies three ways at once, that God will not repent of the evil he had threatened to Saul in taking away the kingdom, nor of the good he had promised to David in giving it, nor of his purpose and promise to Israel to protect and defend them and continue them a nation and kingdom, and that for the confirmation of all this the title of the Strength of Israel is given him. The second confession he compares with the first, that Saul had said as much before but had attended it with an extenuation of his sin, pleading the fear of the people in excuse, whereas here it is without any such plea; and yet by what follows it appears to be not ingenuous and sincere but hypocritical. Samuel's return he defends as he defended the refusal, that though he had said he would not, yet he did, changing his mind as he might without being chargeable with a lie, and he may also have had an impulse from the Lord to do it; and Gill is careful about the motive, that he did not go in order to worship with Saul, which it does not appear he did but rather the contrary, but that Saul might not be despised by the people and his authority lessened while he continued king, and that Samuel might do what Saul had neglected.

Clarke reads the request for pardon literally and then theologically: the Hebrew is bear my sin, take it away, so that Saul asks forgiveness for what he has done against Samuel and asks him to be his intercessor with God, that God may forgive his offence against him, and to turn again with him that he may worship the Lord. The refusal he gives in the plainest terms, that Samuel cannot acknowledge him as king seeing the Lord has rejected him. On the declaration of irreversibility he is brief and absolute, that what God has purposed he will bring to pass, having all power in the heavens and in the earth, and that he will not repent, that is, will not change his purpose, concerning Saul. But Clarke then enters a partial defence of the king which the others do not: we may say, he writes, that it was some extenuation of Saul's fault that the people insisted on preserving the best of the prey, for who could resist the demands of a victorious mob; yet his crime was in consenting, since had he not consented the crime would have been theirs alone. Wesley takes the strongest line of any in Saul's favour, and takes it twice. It does by no means appear, he says, that Saul acts the hypocrite in assigning a false cause of his disobedience; rather he nakedly declares the thing as it was. And of the request for pardon, neither can it be proved that there was any hypocrisy in this; rather charity requires us to believe that he sincerely desired pardon both from God and man, as he now knew he had sinned against both. Samuel's refusal and subsequent return Wesley defends as no lie, since the prophet spoke what he meant and his words and intentions agreed together, though afterwards he saw reason to change his intentions; and he draws a pastoral application from it, that this may relieve many perplexed consciences who think themselves obliged to do what they have said they would do though they see just cause to change their minds. On the sentence of rejection he enters a caution of his own, that the prophet does not say God has rejected Saul from salvation, and asks who besides has authority to say so. The title in the declaration he expounds as supplying the reason why God neither will nor can lie, since lying proceeds from the sense of a man's weakness, who often cannot accomplish his design without lying and dissimulation, for which very reason many princes have used it, whereas God needs no such artifices and can do whatsoever he pleases by his absolute power; and repentance likewise is an effect of weakness and imperfection either of wisdom or of power, so that the word is not here used in the sense it bears earlier in the chapter. Samuel's turning again he explains by two reasons together, first that the people might not upon pretence of this sentence of rejection withdraw their obedience to their sovereign, whereby they would both have sinned against God and have been as sheep without a shepherd, and second that he might rectify Saul's error and execute God's judgment upon Agag.

Henry says Saul is at length brought to put himself into the dress of the penitent, but that it is too evident he only acts the part of a penitent and is not one indeed, since it was with much ado that he was made sensible of his fault and not till he was threatened with being deposed, which touched him in a tender part, so that his confession was not free nor ingenuous but extorted by the rack. He gives several bad signs of the hypocrisy of that repentance, which he says came short even of Ahab's. First, Saul made his application to Samuel only, and seemed most solicitous to stand right in his opinion and gain his favour, making a little god of him in order to preserve his own reputation with the people, who all knew Samuel to be a prophet and the instrument of Saul's preferment; and thinking it would please Samuel he put it into his confession that he had transgressed the commandment of the Lord and Samuel's word, as if Samuel had been in God's stead, whereas David, though convinced by Nathan's ministry, had in his confession his eye to God alone and said that against God only had he sinned. Saul also applies to Samuel for forgiveness, as if any could forgive sin but God only, from which Henry draws that those wretchedly deceive themselves who, having fallen into scandalous sin, think it enough to make their peace with the church and their ministers by a plausible profession of repentance without taking care to make their peace with God by the sincerity of it; the most charitable construction he can put upon it is to suppose that Saul looked upon Samuel as a sort of mediator and intended an address to God in his application to him, but he calls it very weak either way. Second, Saul excused his fault even in the confession of it, which is never the fashion of a true penitent, pleading that he feared the people and obeyed their voice; and Henry thinks the excuse false and frivolous, since there is reason enough to think the thing was purely his own doing, and since by what has been read before it is plain he knew how to keep up his authority among them and did not stand in any awe of them, so that whatever he pretended he did not really fear the people. It is common, Henry adds, for sinners in excusing their faults to plead the thoughts and workings of their own minds, because those are things which, however groundless, no man can disprove, forgetting that God searches the heart. Third, all his care was to save his credit and preserve his interest in the people, lest they should revolt from him or at least despise him, which is why he courts Samuel so earnestly to turn again with him and assist in a public thanksgiving, and why he laid hold on the skirt of his mantle to detain him, not that he cared for Samuel but that he feared the people would forsake him if Samuel did; and Henry observes that many seem zealously affected to good ministers and good people only for the sake of their own interest and reputation while in heart they hate them. The second confession he finds grossest of all: I have sinned, yet honour me before my people, is not the language of a penitent but the contrary, since a penitent would say rather, I have sinned, shame me now, for to me belongs shame, and no man can loathe me so much as I loathe myself; yet how often, Henry says, do we meet with the copies of this hypocrisy, since it is very common for those who are convicted of sin to show themselves very solicitous to be honoured before the people, whereas he that has lost the honour of an innocent can pretend to no other than that of a penitent, and it is the honour of a penitent to take shame to himself. What Saul got by these thin shows of repentance Henry then reckons up, and it is nothing. Samuel repeated the sentence, so far was he from giving hope of its repeal, since he that covers his sins shall never prosper; he refused to turn back and turned about to go away, thinking it unfit to countenance one whom God had rejected so far as to join with him in giving thanks for a victory made to serve Saul's covetousness rather than God's glory, though afterwards he did turn again upon further thoughts and probably by divine direction, either to prevent a mutiny among the people or to do justice on Agag, and Henry notes precisely that though Saul worshipped the Lord it is not said that Samuel presided in that worship. The sign Henry treats as providence turning Saul's rudeness to account: when Samuel was turning from him Saul tore his clothes to detain him, so loth was he to part with the prophet, but Samuel put upon this accident a construction which none but a prophet could, making it signify the rending of the kingdom from him, and that, like the tearing, was his own doing; and Henry follows the sign forward, to the neighbour better than he who afterwards cut off the skirt of Saul's robe and to whom Saul then said that he knew he should surely be king, perhaps remembering this very sign. The declaration of irreversibility Henry renders through the versions, the Eternity or Victory of Israel, the holy One, the most noble One, the triumphant King of Israel, and expounds the reason: men are fickle and alter their minds, feeble and cannot effect their purposes, something happening which they could not foresee by which their measures are broken, but with God it is not so.

debates: Whether Saul's repentance was sincere, which is the chapter's sharpest division, where Henry says it is too evident that he only acts the part of a penitent and gives three signs of hypocrisy, that he applied to Samuel only and even confessed against Samuel's word as though the prophet stood in God's stead, that he excused his fault in the very act of confessing it, and that all his care was to save his credit, so that the words I have sinned yet honour me are the contrary of a penitent's; Gill agrees that the confession was made chiefly to get the sentence reversed and that the second, though without the first's excuse, appears from what follows to be hypocritical; against them Wesley holds twice over that it does by no means appear Saul acts the hypocrite, that he nakedly declares the thing as it was, and that no hypocrisy can be proved in the request for pardon, charity requiring us to believe he sincerely desired it of God and man alike; Clarke leans the same way and offers an extenuation, that the people did insist and who could resist a victorious mob, though Saul's crime was in consenting; and Ellicott takes a middle course, allowing that Saul was terribly in earnest and in great fear but holding the earnestness founded on a desire to keep his power.

Who tore the prophet's garment and how, where Delitzsch defends the Hebrew passive and holds that the lappet was torn off accidentally and evidently without any such intention while Saul was trying to hold the prophet back by force, rejecting a proposed correction from the Greek which would make Saul tear it off deliberately; while Ellicott reads the act as the king's own passionate vehemence, Saul laying hold of the old man perhaps even with some violence, and corrects the English besides, since what was seized was not the mantle but the hem of the ordinary tunic worn by the upper classes, the distinctive prophetic mantle being, as he reports from another writer, certainly not in use in Samuel's day.

How the title given to God in the declaration of irreversibility should be rendered, where Ellicott holds that the Hebrew, which is first found in this passage, would be better given as the Changeless One of Israel, and that those who translate it the Victory or the Triumph of Israel are less accurate; Henry collects the renderings of the versions without choosing among them, the Eternity or Victory of Israel, the holy One, the most noble One, the triumphant King of Israel; and Wesley takes the title as itself supplying the reason why God neither will nor can lie, since lying proceeds from a sense of weakness in one who cannot otherwise accomplish his design, whereas God can do whatever he pleases by absolute power.
outliers: Wesley draws a pastoral application from Samuel's changing his mind, that since the prophet spoke what he meant and afterwards saw just cause to change his intention, this may relieve many perplexed consciences who think themselves bound to do whatever they have said they would do.

Henry follows the torn skirt forward to the later history, where the neighbour better than Saul cut off the skirt of Saul's own robe, and Saul then owned that he knew David should surely be king, perhaps remembering this very sign.
themes: And Saul said unto Samuel, I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.
Now therefore, I pray thee, pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord.
And Samuel said unto Saul, I will not return with thee: for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel.
And as Samuel turned about to go away, he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent.
And Samuel said unto him, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.
And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.
Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord thy God.
So Samuel turned again after Saul; and Saul worshipped the Lord.

32.pericope_label: Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately. And Agag said, Surely the bitterness of death is past. And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. Then Samuel went to Ramah; and Saul went up to his house to Gibeah of Saul. And Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul: and the Lord repented that he had made Saul king over Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the execution as the one stern act of judgment still to be done in the midst of the public thanksgiving. The king of the Amalekites had been sentenced to die and Saul had spared him for selfish reasons of his own; and Ellicott declines to discuss at length the apparent harshness of the doom, holding that there were no doubt amply sufficient reasons for the seemingly hard sentence on the people of Amalek, such as their past crimes, their evil example, and the unhappy influence they probably exercised on the surrounding nations, so that weighed in the balance of the divine justice Amalek had been found wanting. He then offers, speaking as he says in all reverence, a theodicy of his own: perhaps this death which was the doom of Amalek was sent in mercy rather than in punishment, mercy to those whom their evil lives might have corrupted with deep corruption, and mercy to themselves in calling them off from greater evils yet to come had they been permitted still to live on in sin. Their king could not be permitted to live, and from Samuel's words Ellicott gathers that even among a wicked race he seems to have been pre-eminent in wickedness. For Saul's motive in preserving him he repeats a suggestion he calls curious but not wholly improbable, that kings, for the honour of their craft, must spare each other; and he notes that there are other instances in the sacred books of prophets and priests acting as the executioners of the divine decrees. Of the manner of the death he reports a suggestion made with some probability, that the words refer to a peculiar form of putting to death like the quartering in vogue during the Middle Ages. Of the final parting he observes that the old friends met once more in life, but that the interview on that occasion was not of Samuel's seeking, nor does it appear that any communication then passed between them, so that when next the seer and the king spoke together the seer belonged to another and a different world; after this, Samuel came no more to Saul bearing messages and commands or giving him counsel and guidance from God, and Saul's kingship, though still one in fact, from this time lost its theocratic relation, God's ambassador being recalled from him. Delitzsch reads Agag's bearing from the Hebrew adverb as a contented and joyous state of mind, and his words not as any special pleasure at the thought of death nor as a heroic contempt of death, but as the conclusion that his life was to be granted him, since he had not been put to death at once and was now about to be presented to the prophet. Of the sentence he gives the grammar, taking the comparative strictly, and of the execution that Samuel pronounced the sentence of death upon him and hewed him in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal.

Gill supposes the order was given to some of Saul's officers, and in Saul's presence, and before all the people met together for the sacrifice. The sentence he reads as covering two bereavements rather than one, since the Hebrew for making childless may be rendered bereaving, and Agag's sword had bereaved the women not of their children only but of their husbands also, making them both childless and widows; by which, Gill says, it appears that he was a cruel prince, and justly died for his own barbarity and wickedness as well as for the sins of his ancestors four hundred years before. The prophet's withdrawal he places at his native town, where his usual residence was. And the closing statement he reads with the Hebrew idiom, that Samuel added not to see Saul, which does not mean that he never saw him again, for he did see him afterwards, but that the meeting was accidental and that Samuel did not go to see him, Saul rather coming to him; and he reports a Jewish commentator's supposition that Samuel may not have seen him even then, but hid his face from him.

Clarke gathers the renderings of Agag's coming: the Greek has trembling, the Hebrew has delicacies, probably with a word for man understood, so that it means a man of delights, a pleasure-taker, while the Latin has him very fat and trembling. His words Clarke takes the other way from the English, noting that almost all the versions render them differently and give the general sense that death is bitter, which seems to him the true meaning. Of the sentence he observes that it appears Agag had forfeited his life by his own personal transgressions and that his death now was the retribution of his cruelties. On the execution he makes two careful distinctions: what Samuel did here he did in his magisterial capacity, and it is not likely that he did it by his own sword but by that of an executioner, since what kings and magistrates and generals do in an official way by their subjects or servants or soldiers they are said to do themselves. Of the parting he meets the apparent contradiction with the later narrative, where Saul went to see Samuel, by observing that this does not affect what is said here, since from this time Samuel had no connection with Saul and never more acknowledged him as king, though he mourned and prayed for him and continued to perform his prophetic functions at his own town and at the school of the prophets. Wesley reads the sentence as evidence of the man's own character, that it appears he was a tyrant guilty of many bloody actions, and thinks this added for the fuller vindication of God's justice, to show that although God did at this time revenge a crime committed by this man's ancestors four hundred years ago, he did not punish an innocent son for his father's crimes but one that persisted in the same evil courses. The execution he grounds in the command, that Samuel did it by divine instinct and in pursuance of God's express order, which, being sinfully neglected by Saul, was now executed by the prophet; but he adds the caution that these are no precedents for private persons to take the sword. The closing statement he glosses as visiting in token of respect or friendship, or seeking counsel from God for Saul, since otherwise Samuel did see him later, though it was not Samuel that came with design to see Saul but Saul that went thither to see Samuel, and that accidentally.

Henry puts the prophet over the kings at the outset. Of the execution he says Samuel destroyed Agag doubtless by such special direction from heaven as none now can pretend to, and that some think he only ordered it to be done, though perhaps he did it with his own hands as a sacrifice to God's injured justice, sacrifices being wont to be cut in pieces. In Agag's coming he finds vain hopes frustrated, reading the manner three ways, that he came in a stately manner to show that he was a king and therefore to be treated with respect, or in a soft effeminate manner as one never used to hardship who could not set the sole of his foot to the ground for tenderness and delicacy, or so as to move compassion; and in his words he finds a man who, having escaped the sword of Saul that man of war, thought himself in no danger from an old prophet, a man of peace. From the words Henry takes two lessons together: that there is bitterness in death and it is terrible to nature, so that divers versions read the words as saying that surely death is bitter and the Greek has Agag come trembling, since death will dismay the stoutest heart; and that many think the bitterness of death is past when it is not so, putting far from them an evil day which is very near, whereas true believers may through grace say it upon good grounds, since though death be not past the bitterness of it is. In the sentence he finds former wicked practices punished, Samuel calling Agag to account not only for the sins of his ancestors but for his own, since his sword had made women childless and he had trodden in the steps of his ancestors' cruelty, as those under him had likely done also, so that all the righteous blood shed by Amalek is justly required of this generation. Henry observes the pairing of the two vices, that Agag who was delicate and luxurious himself was cruel and barbarous to others, and says it is commonly so, since those who are indulgent in their appetites are not less indulgent of their passions; but blood will be reckoned for, and even kings must account to the King of kings for the guiltless blood they shed or cause to be shed. Of the parting he says Samuel took leave of Saul and never came any more to see him, to advise or assist him in any of his affairs, because Saul did not desire his company nor would be advised by him, and he looked upon him as rejected of God and therefore forsook him; and though he might sometimes see him accidentally, he never came to see him out of kindness or respect. Yet he mourned for Saul, and Henry gives three objects of the mourning: he thought it a very lamentable thing that a man who stood so fair for great things should ruin himself so foolishly; he mourned for the bad state of the country, to which Saul was likely to have been so great a blessing but now would prove a curse and a plague; and he mourned for Saul's everlasting state, having no hope of bringing him to repentance, so that when he wept for him it is likely he made supplication, but the Lord had resolved to undo the work of making Saul king and Samuel's prayers prevailed not. From this Henry draws two rules: that we must mourn for the rejection of sinners though we withdraw from them and dare not converse familiarly with them, as the prophet determined to leave his people and go from them and yet to weep day and night for them; and that we must mourn for them though they do not mourn for themselves, since Saul seems unconcerned at the tokens of God's displeasure under which he lay and yet Samuel mourns day and night for him, as Jerusalem was secure when Christ wept over it.

debates: How the word describing Agag's coming should be read, where Clarke reports the Greek giving trembling and the Hebrew delicacies, so that it means a man of delights, while the Latin has him very fat and trembling; Henry offers a choice of three senses, a stately manner to show he was a king, a soft effeminate manner as one never used to hardship, or a manner calculated to move compassion; and Delitzsch takes the word of his mind rather than his gait, a contented and joyous state, since he thought his life was to be granted him, not having been put to death at once.

What Agag's words mean, where Clarke notes that almost all the versions render them differently from the English and give the sense that death is bitter, which he thinks the true meaning; while Henry keeps both senses at once, that there is bitterness in death which will dismay the stoutest heart, the Greek having Agag come trembling, and also that many think the bitterness of death past when it is not so, putting far from them an evil day which is very near.

Who executed the sentence and by what right, where Henry reports that some hold Samuel only ordered it done but thinks he perhaps did it with his own hands as a sacrifice to God's injured justice, and insists it was by such special direction from heaven as none now can pretend to; Clarke separates the questions, making the act magisterial and thinking it not likely Samuel used his own sword but an executioner's, since what magistrates do officially by their servants they are said to do themselves; Wesley grounds it in the express command which Saul had neglected, but warns that these are no precedents for private persons to take the sword; and Ellicott attends to the manner instead, reporting a suggestion that the words describe a particular form of execution like the quartering of the Middle Ages.
outliers: Ellicott offers, speaking as he says in all reverence, the suggestion that the doom of Amalek may have been sent in mercy rather than in punishment, mercy to those whom their evil lives might have corrupted and mercy to themselves in calling them off from greater evils yet to come.
